title: Χαλκεὺς καὶ κυνάριον
titleEn: The Smith and the Little Dog
part: The Smith and the Little Dog (Chambry 345)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 345. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χαλκεὺς εἶχε κύνα, καὶ ὅτε μὲν ἐχάλκευεν, ὁ κύων ἐκοιμᾶτο· ὅτε δὲ ἤσθιεν, παρίστατο αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Chalkeus eiche kyna, kai hote men echalkeuen, ho kyōn ekoimato· hote de ēsthien, paristato autōi.
sentences.l: A smith had a dog, and when he was at his hammering, the dog would sleep; but when he was eating, it would stand beside him.
sentences.n: χαλκεύς is the worker in bronze, and χαλκεύω his hammering at the forge. The imperfects are habitual: this is what happened day after day, not once.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὀστοῦν ῥίψας αὐτῷ εἶπεν· « Ταλαίπωρε, ὑπνῶδες, ὅταν μὲν τὸν ἄκμονα κρούω, ὑπνοῖς· ὅταν δὲ τοὺς ὀδόντας κινήσω, εὐθὺς ἐγείρῃ. »
sentences.tr: Ho de ostoun rhipsas autōi eipen· « Talaipōre, hypnōdes, hotan men ton akmona krouō, hypnois· hotan de tous odontas kinēsō, euthys egeirēi. »
sentences.l: And he, having thrown it a bone, said: « You wretch, you sleepy one, whenever I strike the anvil, you sleep; but whenever I move my teeth, at once you are awake. »
sentences.i: And he threw it a bone and said: « You wretched sleepy creature — when I beat on the anvil you sleep, but the moment my jaws move you are up. »
sentences.n: Two vocatives in a breath, and they agree: ταλαίπωρος is a two-termination adjective, so ταλαίπωρε serves masculine and feminine alike, and ὑπνώδης is an -ης/-ες adjective, whose masculine vocative singular is ὑπνῶδες — the same form as the neuter, but masculine here, with the κύων. The title calls the animal a κυνάριον, a little dog, where the fable's own text says κύων. ὅταν with the subjunctive is for what happens whenever, not on one occasion.

sentences.t: [Ὅτι] τοὺς ὑπνώδεις καὶ ἀργοὺς καὶ ἐξ ἀλλοτρίων πόνων τρεφομένους ὁ μῦθος ἐλέγχει.
sentences.tr: [Hoti] tous hypnōdeis kai argous kai ex allotriōn ponōn trephomenous ho mythos elenchei.
sentences.l: [That] the fable exposes the sleepy and idle, and those fed from the toils of others.
sentences.i: The fable exposes the sleepy and the idle, and those who live off other men's labours.
sentences.n: Chambry prints Ὅτι in square brackets, his mark for a word he judges to have crept in later and would delete. Because he deletes it there is no subordinator left to govern, and the sentence already has its own verb in ἐλέγχει, so the idiomatic line stands free rather than supplying the 'the story shows' that an unbracketed bare Ὅτι would take. On the formula itself, see fable 93 and fable 227.
